strengths: The paper presents a simple, original, and practically meaningful fusion mechanism: CASA augments cross-attention with local causal text-to-text attention while keeping visual tokens outside the language model's main token stream and KV cache. This directly addresses an important efficiency bottleneck in high-resolution and streaming vision-language models.

The empirical case is broad and generally convincing. The authors evaluate both training a VLM from a text-only 2B backbone and adapting a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B model, covering document/chart understanding, OCR, general VQA, video QA, and live video captioning.

Controlled comparisons are a major strength. Under a shared setup, CASA substantially outperforms vanilla and explicitly gated cross-attention, especially on detail-sensitive tasks; the paper also compares three CASA placements, visual-token FFN updates, Q-Former compression levels, layer placement, and input resolution.

The work is appropriately positioned as an Algorithms/General contribution. It does not reach token-insertion performance everywhere, but demonstrates a useful accuracy-efficiency tradeoff rather than relying solely on headline benchmark scores.

The efficiency motivation is supported by theoretical discussion and practical profiling. The single-layer analysis indicates large training-time memory and compute reductions, while the streaming experiments demonstrate much slower memory growth and sustained latency compared with compressed token insertion.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, with helpful architecture and attention-mask diagrams. Training data, schedules, parameter freezing, resolutions, token budgets, hardware, and optimization settings are described in substantial detail.
weaknesses: Several central efficiency comparisons are not fully matched. The token-insertion model is trained with half as many image tokens, fewer text tokens, and lower maximum resolution because the intended configuration does not fit in memory. This establishes a practical limitation but confounds the reported end-to-end training time and accuracy comparisons; matched-resolution throughput estimates or memory-normalized Pareto curves would make the case stronger.

CASA still has material accuracy gaps to token insertion on precisely the fine-grained tasks emphasized by the paper. Relative to the reproduced Qwen2.5-VL model, InfoVQA falls from 71.6 to 59.6, AI2D from 80.1 to 75.1, and MME from 2249 to 1918. Thus, claims that it recovers 'most' performance should be qualified by task.

The evidence for the proposed 'implicit gating' explanation is suggestive rather than conclusive. Masking self-attention only at inference creates a substantial train-test intervention, so the severe degradation does not uniquely establish gating as the causal mechanism. Training matched variants without self keys/values, or comparing learned contribution norms and explicit gates under matched optimization, would better support this interpretation.

The live-captioning evaluation is limited. Its principal quality metric uses GPT-4o-generated references and GPT-4o as judge, lacks uncertainty or human validation, and the best reported CASA score (39.4) remains below LiveCC-7B-Base (43.2). The memory/latency plots are valuable, but longer-duration quality evaluations and matched-backbone streaming baselines would better substantiate the application claim.

No variability across training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite some comparatively small differences among CASA variants. Given the large training scale, even limited multi-seed evidence on the reduced ablation setting would improve confidence.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a usable project-page URL in the supplied manuscript, despite repeated references to it and a promise of released inference code and models. Some dataset-mixture and evaluation details also depend on external repositories, making exact reconstruction harder.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, CASA is a simple, technically plausible fusion mechanism: augmenting cross-attention with causal local text-to-text attention preserves the principal inference advantages of cross-attention while providing an implicit route for regulating visual updates.

The strongest evidence is the controlled comparison in Table 6. With broadly matched training conditions, CASA improves average grouped performance from 40.3 for vanilla cross-attention and 41.5 for gated cross-attention to 63.2–65.4, with especially large gains on document, chart, and OCR tasks.

The evaluation is broad. It covers nine image benchmarks, five video benchmarks, models initialized from both a text-only LLM and a pretrained VLM, three CASA placements, token-compression baselines, image-resolution studies, and multiple architectural ablations.

The paper demonstrates a practically relevant efficiency benefit. Avoiding visual tokens in the LLM FFNs and persistent KV cache substantially reduces training memory and supports much longer streaming runs than insertion baselines. CASA∨ offers an attractive efficiency/performance trade-off.

The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix provides useful implementation information, including data composition, training stages, token budgets, resolutions, parameter-freezing choices, and hardware requirements.
weaknesses: The central claim that CASA nearly closes the insertion gap is overstated. Against the controlled Helium insertion model, the best CASA variant remains about 7% worse on average, with large absolute deficits on ChartQA, InfoVQA, AI2D, and MME. Converting Qwen2.5-VL similarly drops InfoVQA from 71.6 to 59.6 and MME from 2249 to 1918. These are material losses on exactly the fine-grained tasks emphasized by the paper.

The insertion comparison is not fully controlled: insertion models are trained with lower resolution, half as many image tokens, and shorter text sequences because of memory limits. This demonstrates a resource constraint, but it confounds architectural accuracy comparisons and makes the reported end-to-end training times unsuitable as like-for-like efficiency measurements. Equal-resolution/equal-token and equal-compute comparisons are needed.

The streaming-video evidence is substantially weaker than the image evidence. The only quantitative captioning result uses approximately 20-second sports clips, a single GPT-4o judge protocol, and achieves 39.0 versus 43.2 for LiveCC-7B-Base. There is no human evaluation, standard caption metric, uncertainty estimate, or quantitative long-duration quality evaluation, despite long-horizon streaming being a major motivation.

The streaming comparison changes both architecture and backbone: the qualitative insertion baseline is a Q-Former Helium1-2B model, whereas the main CASA captioner adapts Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Moreover, CASA discards direct access to old visual tokens and retains only their textual consequences. Constant visual-memory cost therefore comes with an unmeasured loss of retrospective visual access; long-video retrieval, temporal reasoning, and forgetting should be evaluated.

The proposed explanation as implicit gating is suggestive rather than established. Masking self-attention only at inference creates a severe train–test intervention, so the resulting collapse does not isolate gating as the causal mechanism. Attention magnitude is also not equivalent to contribution magnitude. Comparisons against learned scalar/vector gates, residual scaling, and other matched identity-preserving controls would make this conclusion convincing.

Benchmark contamination is insufficiently addressed. Training uses large curated mixtures overlapping many task domains and explicitly includes datasets such as GQA, but the paper reports no train/test deduplication or leakage analysis for the nine evaluation benchmarks. This is particularly important for document, chart, and OCR benchmarks that motivate the contribution.

Some efficiency reporting needs correction or clarification. Table 11 labels the token counts as 50/1024 image/text while its caption states 1024 image and 50 text; several headline measurements are single runs without variability; and the practical tests do not report throughput or quality under a common end-to-end memory/latency budget.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix: the paper promises inference code and trained models, but not the full training implementation, and omits several optimizer and schedule details. Reproducing the main results also requires roughly 64 H100 GPUs for multiple days.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, CASA is a simple, technically plausible modification: allowing local causal text-to-text attention within the visual fusion layer preserves the scalability advantages of cross-attention while substantially improving fine-grained visual understanding.

The controlled ablation is compelling: under the same reduced training setup, CASA reaches a 65.4 grouped average versus 40.3 for vanilla cross-attention and 41.5 for gated cross-attention, with especially large gains on document, chart, and OCR tasks.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering nine image benchmarks, five video benchmarks, three architectural variants, training from a text-only LLM, and conversion of a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL model. Adapting a frozen VLM is practically useful and recovers much of the original model's performance.

The efficiency motivation is well aligned with the architecture. Image tokens avoid the LLM feed-forward layers and persistent KV cache, and the paper provides theoretical analysis, profiling, training resource measurements, and streaming latency/memory experiments.

Ablations examine CASA placement, image-feature updates, token compression, resolution, training progress, and attention behavior. The paper is clearly written, visually polished, and provides substantial implementation and training detail.
weaknesses: The proposed explanation of CASA as implicit gating is not conclusively established. Masking self-attention only after training creates an out-of-distribution intervention and is not equivalent to training a model without that path; large self-attention weights likewise do not by themselves demonstrate causal gating. A trained self-only or learned-gate control would make the mechanism claim more convincing.

Several headline comparisons are not fully controlled. In Table 2, CASA processes roughly 0.3T training tokens versus 0.1T for the insertion baseline, while the methods also use different training resolutions and sequence limits. Comparisons to external cross-attention models differ in architecture and data. These results establish practical competitiveness but isolate the architectural benefit less cleanly than the presentation suggests.

The efficiency evaluation needs more apples-to-apples end-to-end measurements. Table 1 gives insertion a reduced sequence length because of memory limits, Table 11 profiles only a single synthetic layer, and CASA-plus can be slightly slower than insertion at inference in that microbenchmark. The streaming plots do not clearly specify matched backbones, output lengths, quality, or uncertainty, and omit strong KV-eviction or streaming-memory baselines.

The live-captioning evidence is comparatively weak: the 3B model remains below the strongest reported LiveCC baselines, evaluation relies on GPT-4o as both reference generator and judge without variance or human validation, and the qualitative outputs contain conspicuous hallucinations and contradictions. This section demonstrates feasibility and efficiency more convincingly than caption quality.

CASA still shows meaningful accuracy gaps to token insertion, particularly on InfoVQA, AI2D, and chart/document understanding—the very fine-detail regime emphasized by the paper. The Qwen adaptation loses about 12 points on InfoVQA and over 300 MME points, so claims that it nearly closes the gap should be qualified.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the submitted manuscript: it promises code, models, and a project page, yet the project-page URL is blank. Some reporting details are also inconsistent, such as the image/text token ordering around Table 11, and no multi-seed variability or statistical significance is provided.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as Concept & Feasibility with an Applied/Systems component rather than primarily as a new-algorithm paper. Under that framing, revisiting cross-attention through controlled modern training pipelines is a useful and timely contribution.

The decomposition of cross-attention versus token insertion into five design differences (D1-D5) is clear and insightful. It connects parameter sharing, joint text-image attention, layer placement, image-token updates, and visual-history retention to concrete efficiency and accuracy trade-offs.

The strongest evidence is the controlled Helium1-2B comparison: models share the backbone, vision encoder, public training data, token budget, and training horizon. Across nine image benchmarks, vanilla cross-attention is generally close to insertion, while Table 1 demonstrates substantial training-memory and streaming-inference advantages.

The adaptation experiment is practically valuable: adding cross-attention to Qwen2.5-VL-3B while freezing most pretrained parameters retains much of its image and video capability. The paper also compares against recent cross-attention models and evaluates multiple architectural variants, image resolutions, layer frequencies, token compression, and image-token FFN updates.

The streaming application illustrates a meaningful use case where discarding old visual keys and values is structurally beneficial. The manuscript is generally well organized, technically understandable, and unusually forthcoming about weaknesses on fine-grained chart and document tasks. Training data, schedules, resolutions, optimization, and compute are documented reasonably well.
weaknesses: The streaming evidence is considerably weaker than the broad practical claims. LiveSports3K contains only approximately 20-second clips; caption quality is measured solely by a GPT-4o judge without uncertainty estimates or human validation; and the proposed 3B model scores 39.0% versus 43.2% for LiveCC-7B-Base. Longer-horizon quality is not quantitatively evaluated, even though indefinite streaming is a central motivation.

The claim of near-constant memory needs qualification: visual KV memory is bounded, but the text KV cache still grows as captions and per-frame delimiter/gist tokens accumulate. Figure 4(b) plots wall time rather than the memory trajectory repeatedly referenced in the text. A direct memory-versus-duration plot, exact OOM points, and comparisons with competitive eviction or bounded-memory streaming baselines would make the systems claim convincing.

The insertion baseline used for long streaming retains visual tokens indefinitely, making its eventual slowdown and OOM largely expected. Q-Former compression is tested, but stronger alternatives discussed in related work—frame pruning, cache compression, sliding windows, and explicit visual memories—are not compared. The paper therefore establishes an architectural advantage over naive persistent insertion more clearly than an advantage over the best streaming insertion systems.

Some efficiency reporting is under-specified or potentially difficult to interpret. Table 1 does not fully expose the tested sequence composition, total parameter counts, FLOPs, cache precision, batch size, and latency breakdown. Training throughput is reported in text tokens per second despite very large and variant-dependent visual computation. The controlled insertion run also uses half-length sequences with doubled accumulation, which matches aggregate token counts but not necessarily the distribution of contexts or optimization dynamics.

Several conclusions rely on single runs and point estimates, with no variance, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to data order and initialization. This is especially important for small benchmark differences among cross-attention variants and for the LLM-as-judge results.

The proposed gist mechanism is only implicit: one existing post-image delimiter token per frame is assumed to preserve past visual content, but there is no direct ablation against no gist token, multiple learned gist tokens, or explicit visual-history retention. Consequently, the explanation that strong video performance arises from stored information in gist tokens is plausible but not established.

The qualitative live-caption examples expose notable hallucinations and contradictions—for example, describing a pangolin first as a reptile and then as a mammal, and producing dubious Apollo-related narration. These examples weaken confidence in deployment-oriented claims and merit a more systematic analysis of temporal consistency and hallucination.

Reproducibility is good at the configuration level but incomplete in the supplied manuscript: the project-page URL is blank, the release statement emphasizes inference code and trained models rather than the complete training pipeline, and exact evaluation prompts/settings for the judge are not fully reproduced. There is also no explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion concerning streaming caption hallucinations and accessibility use cases.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: visual-token insertion makes long and streaming multimodal contexts expensive, while cross-attention offers a plausible efficiency advantage.

The controlled Helium1-2B comparison is valuable: cross-attention and insertion models use the same backbone, vision encoder, public training data, and broadly matched training budgets. Results across nine image benchmarks show that vanilla cross-attention can be substantially more competitive than comparisons between unrelated published models suggest.

The decomposition into five differences between cross-attention and insertion is a useful conceptual framework. The paper also examines parameter sharing, replacement of self-attention layers, joint text-visual attention, image-token updates, and token compression rather than reporting only one favored configuration.

Evaluation is reasonably broad, covering document/OCR, general VQA, video QA, training efficiency, inference memory, latency, and live captioning. The appendix provides useful training schedules, data composition, resolutions, optimization settings, and parameter-freezing details. weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that criterion, originality is limited: vanilla cross-attention, parameter sharing, alternating/replacing attention layers, Q-Former compression, and visual FFN updates are established ideas. The D1-D5 decomposition is helpful but mainly taxonomic, and the strongest contribution is an empirical re-evaluation rather than a new method.

The central streaming-quality evidence is not convincing enough. LiveSports3K is evaluated only with an LLM judge, without uncertainty, human validation, standard captioning metrics, or an insertion-based model trained and evaluated under the same backbone, data, and compute. The principal baselines are differently sized 7B systems, so the experiment does not isolate the effect of fusion architecture.

The qualitative live-captioning results expose serious semantic errors—for example, the pangolin example calls the animal a reptile before calling it a mammal, while the Apollo example contains an incoherent account of “40 years of space camp missions.” These samples undermine the practical claim, yet caption factuality and hallucination are not analyzed.

The claimed preservation of video history through ordinary post-image delimiter tokens is insufficiently substantiated. There is no ablation removing these tokens, varying their number, comparing them with explicitly trained gist tokens, or probing what information they retain. Moreover, the video comparison changes both the attention window and maximum frame budget, complicating attribution.

Efficiency reporting is narrower than the conclusions imply. Measurements use one 2B backbone and one GPU, while essential conditions such as precision, batch size, exact sequence/frame lengths, decoding settings, and kernel configuration are not fully reported alongside Table 1 and Figure 4. There is no comparison with strong streaming insertion baselines using cache eviction, pruning, or memory compression, although these are discussed in related work. Memory is also not truly constant because the textual KV cache continues to grow.

Performance gaps remain substantial on fine-grained visual tasks: adapting Qwen2.5-VL drops InfoVQA from 75.1 to 57.4 and also degrades DocVQA, AI2D, and MME. The paper acknowledges this but does not diagnose why it occurs or test remedies, limiting the general claim that cross-attention retains the base model’s capabilities.

The experiments report single point estimates without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Several comparisons use reproduced scores while others use published scores, and the insertion baseline requires different sequence lengths and gradient accumulation; these choices may be reasonable but leave residual uncertainty in claims based on differences of only a few points.

Reproducibility and presentation need improvement: the project-page URL is absent, exact evaluation prompts and decoding settings are not specified, and the paper contains numerous grammatical and typesetting errors. These are secondary to the evidence issues but make the study harder to verify.

strengths: The paper makes a timely and practically important case for reconsidering cross-attention in vision-language models. Its central controlled comparison is valuable: when trained in the same modern pipeline, vanilla cross-attention trails token insertion by only a modest average margin while substantially reducing streaming inference costs.

The decomposition into five architectural differences between cross-attention and token insertion is clear and useful. The variants involving parameter sharing, local joint text-visual attention, layer replacement, image-token updates, and visual history provide a coherent framework for understanding the performance-efficiency trade-off.

The empirical study is broad, covering two starting points—a text-only Helium1-2B model and pretrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B—as well as image, video-QA, and live-captioning settings. The matched Helium comparison is particularly convincing, with CA remaining close to insertion on most benchmarks and the paper candidly identifying larger gaps on chart and infographic understanding.

The efficiency results demonstrate a meaningful application-level benefit rather than relying solely on theoretical complexity. Cross-attention avoids accumulating visual tokens in the language-model KV cache, producing much better memory and latency behavior over long streaming sequences.

The paper includes relevant architectural ablations, token-compression comparisons, training details, resolution studies, and convergence curves. The planned release of inference code and trained models further supports reproducibility.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear; figures and tables make the architecture and trade-offs easy to follow. weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: vanilla cross-attention, parameter sharing, image-token FFN updates, and token compression are largely established ideas. The main contribution is therefore best understood as a careful empirical reassessment and practical systems study, rather than a fundamentally new fusion algorithm.

The strongest comparisons to prior cross-attention models are not controlled for backbone, training data, resolution, or optimization. They show that the proposed training recipe yields a strong CA model, but do not isolate whether improvements over mPLUG-Owl3 or StreamChat arise from the fusion mechanism itself. The within-pipeline CA-versus-insertion experiments provide the more defensible evidence.

The efficiency evaluation lacks several details needed to reproduce or interpret absolute values, including memory units in Table 1, precise sequence dimensions and batch settings, numerical parameter counts, precision and kernel configuration, and a direct accounting of total training compute. Figure 4 reports wall time and OOM points but not the full memory trajectory emphasized in the text.

The phrase “near-constant memory” should be qualified: cross-attention removes growth from visual KV entries, but the textual KV cache still grows with generated or transcript tokens. Likewise, latency in Figure 4 is substantially flatter than insertion but not strictly constant.

The live-captioning quality evidence is comparatively weak. It uses a single LLM-as-judge win-rate protocol without uncertainty estimates or detailed judge settings, remains below the strongest reported LiveCC baselines, and provides only a few qualitative examples. Some examples contain conspicuous hallucinations or contradictions, such as describing a pangolin first as a reptile and then as a mammal, which is relevant to the claimed practical application.

Several ablations are imperfectly isolated. In particular, the image-update experiment freezes the vision encoder and uses a smaller-scale setup, so its performance difference cannot be attributed solely to FFN updates. No repeated-training variance or significance analysis is provided.

The training mixture is very large and heterogeneous, but the paper does not report an explicit evaluation-set decontamination check. Some optimization and evaluation details—such as AdamW coefficients, weight decay, warmup/decay lengths, decoding settings, and exact judge prompts—are also omitted. These are remediable reproducibility issues rather than flaws that overturn the main result.
